body.text: In the U.S. state of Hawai‘i, Iris lives far from the pressures of urban China. Growing up in Zhejiang, she spent much of her childhood on what her mother called “self-improvement”: Olympiad math, piano lessons, and daily swimming. After graduating from New York University (NYU), Iris chose a simple, quiet life in Hawai‘i, using geographic distance to protect her personal autonomy from the pressure facing Chinese women in their 20s to settle down, marry, and have children.

Halfway across the world, Jessica is confronting the same expectations from within China. After studying in Shanghai and Europe and working at an international organization in New York, where a mentor once urged her to stop working late and “enjoy the New York night,” Jessica returned to China to finish her master’s thesis and enter the domestic job market. There, she met a second, more intimate pressure: the expectation that she should marry and have children. Rather than quietly accepting it, she confronted the idea directly, over dinner with her mother, asking: “Are you actually happy in your own marriage? What has it genuinely brought you?”

Iris and Jessica belong to a highly educated cohort of young Chinese women whose lives are unfolding alongside a demographic problem the state is eager to solve. Facing an aging population, a shrinking workforce, and historically low fertility rates, Beijing introduced the Three-Child Policy in 2021, allowing Chinese couples to have up to three children. China’s government has since increasingly emphasized marriage and childbearing as social priorities.

Yet China’s demographic crisis gained steam during the same decades of modernization that gave women access to more education, higher incomes, and greater mobility. That means women like Iris and Jessica have more reasons, and more means, to delay or reconsider marriage and motherhood.

Research on China’s education expansion by Jiwei Chen and Jiangying Guo of Nanjing Agricultural University found that increased female education can delay entry into marriage and childbirth and reduce fertility, in part by raising the opportunity costs of childrearing. The modernization that expanded women’s choices has made the traditional sequence of adulthood – marry, have children, settle near family – less inevitable.

Jessica confronts this tension directly, pressing her own mother on whether marriage delivered what it promised and treating parenthood as a choice to question rather than a milestone to check off. Iris resists more obliquely: rather than arguing with the assumption that a good daughter eventually settles down close to home, she puts enough distance (first New York, then Hawai‘i) between herself and the people who would enforce the traditional path, letting their expectations fade into background noise instead of demands she has to answer.
Neither is rejecting family, marriage, or children outright. Both are refusing to treat any of these options as the default for a Chinese woman.
Jessica: Deconstructing the Script

Upon returning to China to finish her thesis, Jessica found the job hunt less a search for a career than a reckoning with what kind of life she was willing to accept. In Europe and New York, she’d grown used to a workplace culture defined by what she calls “松弛感”: ease, dignity, being treated first as a person. One night, working late in New York, her mentor stopped her: “You are in New York. You should go enjoy the night.” The line stuck with her.

The anecdote formed a sharp contrast with Jessica’s internship at a major Chinese internet company, where a hyper-competitive, results-only culture left people passing their anxiety down the hierarchy.

She posted a comparison of the two experiences on Xiaohongshu and it sparked a fight in the comments: some dismissed it as a naive “student mindset”; others agreed with a Chinese woman writing from Europe, who argued that Western employers need their workers enough to treat them decently, while Chinese managers can simply replace anyone who underperforms.
For Jessica, the real question was how much room there was for personal choice to override social norms. That questioning carried over from professional pressures straight into marriage.

Years abroad had sharpened her sense of independence, but her father still pictured a conventional future for her, and relatives kept the pressure alive by mentioning which of her peers had already married. Jessica pushed back on the premise itself, arguing that a mother-daughter bond can matter as much as a marital one. She half-jokingly tells relatives that if marriage is unavoidable, it’s better to get in and out of it quickly than drag out something broken.

The same skepticism shapes how she thinks about children. She’s fond of them but treats parenthood as a serious undertaking that shouldn’t simply follow marriage on a fixed timeline. She has watched enough families to conclude that unhappy marriages, and kids who are under-supported despite material comfort, are more common than the success stories that get celebrated. Teenagers hit adolescence with mental health struggles, some withdrawing from school, often because parents were too consumed by work to be present.
Jessica has also watched women of her mother’s generation absorb the burden of family life, reshaping careers around husbands and children. She has no intention of doing the same by default.

That came to a head at a family dinner, when marriage came up again and Jessica turned the question back on her mother: was she actually happy in her marriage? What had it given her? It was an invitation to examine whether women’s sacrifices for family are as inevitable as they’re made to seem.

“If my pain can never be carried by anyone else,” Jessica told The Diplomat, “then my happiness has to be mine to build, too.” She’s stopped ruling out partners by age, and increasingly by nationality; a good match is rare enough without narrowing the field further. Her mother has softened too, no longer pressing on timelines.

None of this makes her anti-marriage or anti-motherhood. But Jessica insists on the right to decide what place they hold in her life, rather than letting either define her adulthood before she’s had the chance to define it herself.
Iris: Exiting the Room

Growing up in Zhejiang, Iris Liu’s school breaks were a rotation of enrichment classes: Olympiad math, swimming, roller skating, dance, painting, piano. As an only child, she absorbed her mother’s conviction that giving her every possible advantage was simply what good parenting looked like. Before Iris had even reached middle school, her mother was already telling her she needed to learn to swim: American Ivy League universities, she’d heard, liked students who could swim. The plan was always aimed outward, toward a future far from home.
Years later, Iris would indeed leave China. She just wouldn’t use that mobility the way her mother had imagined.

The first crack came early, almost by accident. A two-week middle-school trip to Los Angeles was supposed to preview the life her mother was preparing her for. Instead, Iris came home unimpressed: a suburban campus, cafeteria pizza, none of the excitement she’d expected. Her disappointment rippled into her mother’s plans: the pressure around swimming eased, and the push toward an international high-school track quietly faded. Still, the broader trajectory held.

Iris went on to NYU, and after graduation had the kind of options her education was supposed to produce: interviews for corporate jobs with six-figure salaries. She did not end up in any of these. She chose instead a job in Hawai‘i.

Her parents had a particular idea of success. When Iris told them about interviews with major firms with salaries over $100,000 a year, they barely reacted. Her father countered instead with a story about a colleague’s child who’d quit an investment-banking job after three years, burned out. It was meant to be a cautionary tale about what a prestigious career actually costs. What her parents want for Iris is harder to define than pure career success. They want her to have a manageable life, to be somewhere stable, and eventually to come home.

That expectation rarely arrives as a demand; it shows up in small comments instead. While Iris was in New York, her father compared New York’s infrastructure unfavorably to Shanghai’s. Her mother notes that Hangzhou “isn’t so bad” whenever Iris complains about where she’s living. When Iris mentions a hard week at work, the response is often some version of: why not just come home, find something stable?

Nothing is framed as an ultimatum, and her parents insist the choice is hers, but the suggestions add up to a recognizable idea of what adulthood should eventually look like: stop drifting, settle, put down roots – back in China, of course.

In China, the idea of settling down is hard to separate from marriage. For women in their 20s, stability tends to arrive bundled with questions about where they’ll live, whom they’ll marry, when they’ll start a family. Distance, Iris has found, gives her room to answer those questions on her own schedule.
“In China, there is a pervasive pressure on women in their 20s to quickly find stability, buy an apartment, and marry,” she says. “In Hawai‘i, that marital clock simply vanishes.”

That doesn’t mean the tension disappears, only that it changes shape. Iris is living inside one social world while carrying the expectations of another. The norms around her carry no real urgency about marrying or settling permanently. Her family’s expectations carry plenty. If she followed the culture in her new home, Iris risks feeling like she’s failing her family, but trying to import her family’s values wholesale doesn’t fit the life she’s actually building.

“It’s a little like being caught in the middle,” she said. “The values your family brings with them don’t completely fit the society you’re living in, but you can’t just stop caring about what your family thinks either.”

Iris still sometimes looks at friends her age who are marrying, buying homes, building linear careers, and wonders if she’s falling behind. Her own path has zigzagged instead: an exchange year in Japan, an unplanned application to NYU, offers turned down, a move to Hawai‘i with no five-year plan attached. But the uncertainty isn’t a side effect of her choices – it’s part of what she’s choosing.

Her parents spent years investing in an education meant to expand what was possible for Iris. She did become educated, and mobile. She simply redefined what that mobility was for: not a way of moving closer to the life her family imagined, but a way of gaining enough distance to decide, on her own, whether that life was ever really what she wanted.

Where Jessica confronts the script by questioning it at the dinner table, Iris resists it by leaving the room – going far enough away that she can still hear her family’s expectations without having to obey them.
Choosing to Choose

Jessica and Iris didn’t set out to make a political statement. Jessica wanted a job, and a marriage, that didn’t consume her; Iris wanted a life she’d actually chosen rather than one assembled for her since childhood, class by enrichment class.

They are both ultimately resisting the assumption that a woman’s education and independence are ultimately in service of marriage, children, and “settling down,” rather than choices she gets to make, or decline, on her own terms.

Their parents invested in swimming lessons and Olympiad math and study abroad because those things were supposed to expand what their daughters could become – and they did, just not in the direction their families expected.

Marriage and motherhood remain open questions for both of them. Their parents will keep aging, friends will keep marrying, and the clock Iris describes may eventually start ticking. Neither woman claims to know what they will ultimately decide. But the fact that they see marriage and motherhood as a choice at all – something that can be embraced or refused – is already a small revolution in and of itself.
